subject: ela
skillName: Develop and strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing
description: Students develop and strengthen their writing by planning before they write, revising to improve content and organization, editing to correct conventions, rewriting weak parts, and trying a new approach when a draft is not working. They identify which stage of the writing process a task belongs to, recognize what a piece of writing needs next, choose the revision that most improves clarity, focus, organization, word choice, or sentence flow, and choose the edit that corrects a convention error without changing meaning. Because this is a writing standard, every item embeds the full prompt, sentence, paragraph, or short draft it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of the writing process through analysis, selection, and short revision rather than full multi-paragraph essays.
subSkills: Distinguish the stages of the writing process (planning or prewriting, drafting, revising, editing, rewriting) and identify which stage a given action belongs to
Plan writing by selecting a focused topic, gathering and grouping relevant ideas, and ordering them with an outline or organizer before drafting
Revise for content and focus by adding missing support, cutting details that do not fit the topic, or sharpening a vague main idea
Revise for organization by reordering sentences or paragraphs and adding transitions so ideas flow logically
Revise for clarity and word choice by replacing vague, repeated, or weak words with precise ones and combining choppy sentences
Edit for conventions by correcting errors in spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and grammar without changing the writer's meaning
Recognize when a draft is not working and decide to rewrite a section or try a new approach rather than make small fixes
Tell the difference between revising (changing ideas, content, and organization) and editing (correcting surface conventions)

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the writing-process stage
problemArchetypes.example: Read the action described in the item: 'Before writing, Mia lists every idea she has about her topic and then circles the three she likes best.' Which stage of the writing process is Mia in? Options: planning, revising, editing, publishing. Answer: planning, because she is gathering and organizing ideas before drafting.

problemArchetypes.name: Revise versus edit
problemArchetypes.example: Read the change a writer made: 'The writer moved the last sentence of the paragraph to the beginning so the main idea comes first.' Is this revising or editing? Answer: revising, because changing the order to improve organization affects the content and structure, not just surface conventions.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best revision for clarity or word choice
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence embedded in the item: 'The dog was very big and the dog ran very fast.' Which revision is the strongest improvement? Options: (A) 'The big dog ran fast.' (B) 'The huge dog raced across the yard.' (C) 'The dog was big and fast.' (D) 'The dog, which was big, ran.' Answer: B, because it replaces the vague repeated words with precise language and combines the ideas smoothly.

problemArchetypes.name: Add the missing support
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short paragraph in the item that states 'Recycling helps our town' but gives no reasons. Which sentence best develops the paragraph? Answer: a sentence that adds a specific reason or example such as 'Recycling keeps plastic out of the local river,' not a sentence that repeats the main idea or adds an off-topic detail.

problemArchetypes.name: Cut the sentence that does not belong
problemArchetypes.example: Read the paragraph embedded in the item about how plants need sunlight to grow; one sentence says 'My uncle has a blue car.' Which sentence should the writer remove during revision? Answer: the sentence about the blue car, because it does not support the paragraph's topic about plants and sunlight.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the edit that corrects a convention error
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence in the item: 'me and my friend goes to the park on saturday.' Which edited version is correct? Answer: 'My friend and I go to the park on Saturday,' which fixes capitalization, subject pronoun, and verb agreement without changing the meaning.

problemArchetypes.name: Decide the next step or a new approach
problemArchetypes.example: Read the draft note in the item: 'A writer has tried twice to fix a confusing paragraph by changing single words, but readers still cannot follow it.' What should the writer do next? Answer: rewrite the paragraph or try a new approach, because small word fixes have not solved the problem.

Easy.description: A single sentence or a short described action (roughly 8 to 25 words total) embedded in the item, with a clearly stated task. The task is identify-level: name which stage of the writing process an action belongs to, decide whether a change is revising or editing in an obvious case, or pick the one clearly better word or fix. Only one component is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or a one-line described action included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (process stage, revise vs edit, single word swap, one clear convention fix)
Identify-level task: label or select, no multi-part judgment required
Distractors are clearly weaker (a wrong stage that does not match the action, an unrelated word, an option that adds a new error)

Medium.description: A short paragraph or a two to four sentence draft (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: choose the revision that best improves clarity, focus, or word choice; identify which sentence should be cut or added to develop the paragraph; or choose the edit that corrects a convention error among plausible options. The student must weigh more than one option that is partly defensible.
constraints: Stimulus is a short paragraph or a brief multi-sentence draft in the prompt
Tests revision for content, organization, clarity, word choice, or a convention edit in context
Analyze-level task: choose or revise based on how well the change improves the writing
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a revision that fixes one issue but adds another, a cut of a sentence that actually belongs, an edit that changes meaning)

Hard.description: A multi-sentence draft paragraph (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item, often containing more than one weakness or a draft that is not working. The task is evaluate-level: decide which revision most improves the paragraph as a whole, judge whether the writer should make small fixes or rewrite and try a new approach, choose the best reordering of sentences for logical flow, or determine why a revision fails and what would strengthen the draft. Requires inference about the writer's purpose and how the parts of the draft fit together.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 6 sentence draft paragraph included in the prompt
Tests how multiple components interact: focus, support, organization, clarity, conventions, and the choice to rewrite
Evaluate-level task: select the best overall revision or next step and justify it against the whole draft
Requires inference to judge logical flow, what the draft still needs, and whether small fixes or a new approach is warranted

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses editing with revising, treating a deep content or organization change as a simple surface correction
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'moved a paragraph to improve organization' or 'added a supporting reason' as editing, instead of recognizing it as revising

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses revising with editing, treating a surface convention fix as a content change
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'fixed a spelling error' or 'added a missing capital letter' as revising, instead of recognizing it as editing

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misidentifies the writing-process stage, matching an action to a stage by a surface word rather than its purpose
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls listing and grouping ideas before drafting 'revising' or calls correcting punctuation in a finished draft 'planning'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks any added sentence develops a paragraph, ignoring whether it supports the topic
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an off-topic or repeated sentence as the best way to develop a paragraph because it sounds detailed, rather than a sentence that adds relevant support

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a relevant sentence as the one to cut, removing useful support instead of the off-topic detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a sentence that actually supports the main idea for removal, leaving the irrelevant sentence in the paragraph

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a revision that adds a new error or changes the writer's meaning while fixing the original problem
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an edited sentence that corrects one mistake but introduces a new grammar error or alters what the writer was trying to say

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student keeps making tiny word fixes when a draft needs a rewrite, mistaking small edits for real improvement
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses to swap a single word in a paragraph that readers cannot follow, instead of rewriting the section or trying a new approach

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student values longer or fancier wording over clearer wording, choosing wordy or repetitive revisions
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a revision that adds extra words or repeats the idea as the strongest, instead of the concise, precise version that improves clarity
